extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theology, church-state relations, and ecclesiastical history
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical exposition of the origin, nature, and limits of ecclesiastical offices, ordination, revenue, and authority in the apostolic and early-church period, and their relation to civil sovereign power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of Councils are not Laws without civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acts of Councell of the Apostles, and of other Doctors or Councels assembled without the Authority of the Civill Soveraign, were then no Laws, but Councells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Acts could not bind Christians as laws; they were 'Conditions, proposed to those that sought Salvation' which converts might accept or refuse. Only Kings or Sovereign Assemblies (civil sovereigns) can make such doctrinal rules into laws with coercive force. Thus the New Testament books, though 'most perfect Rules of Christian Doctrine,' 'could not be made Laws' except by civil authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostleship requires being a competent witness of the Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apostleship was distinguished by being 'Witnesses of our Saviours Resurrection' — one must have seen our Saviour after his Resurrection, or have conversed with him before and seen his works and other arguments of his Divinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to explain the necessary property of an Apostle: e.g., Matthias was chosen from those who had companied with the Apostles during Christ's ministry; Paul, though not a disciple before the Passion, saw Christ on the road to Damascus and so qualified as a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordination and election by the congregation (plurality of suffrages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presbyters, Pastors, and first Apostles (after Christ) were elected/ordained by the Assembly/Congregation of Christians in each city, commonly by plurality of votes (cheirotonesantes — 'holding up of hands').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apostles acted as presidents to call assemblies and pronounce election; ordination involved the people choosing by customary means (raised hands, voices, ballots). Examples: Matthias chosen by lot among the congregation; Acts 14.23 'they ordained Elders in every Church' understood as ordaining by the holding up of hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between magisterial and ministerial offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Some ecclesiastical offices are 'Magisteriall' (preaching the Gospel, administering Sacraments, Divine Service, teaching rules of Faith and Manners) while others are 'Ministeriall' (Deacons administering secular necessities of the Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magisteriall offices (Apostles, Bishops, Elders, Pastors, Doctors) carry teaching authority. Ministerial offices serve the congregation's temporal needs; both are 'Ministers' but of different persons (Christ vs the Congregation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishop/Elder/Pastor/Doctor were historically the same office
rubrics_metrics.description: In the time of the Apostles, Bishop, Pastor, Elder, Doctor (Teacher) were 'so many divers names of the same Office'; there was no coercive church government then, only guidance by doctrine and persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Timothy was an Elder and also a Bishop; S. John begins his Second Epistle 'The Elder to the Elect Lady.' The lack of coercive power meant titles were largely synonymous for the office of guiding the flock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evangelists and Prophets are gifts, not fixed offices
rubrics_metrics.description: By the names of Evangelists and Prophets is not signified any Office, but several Gifts by which several men were profitable to the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evangelists wrote accounts (Matthew, John, Mark, Luke); Prophets interpreted the Old Testament or declared special revelations. Gifts (languages, exorcism, healing) do not by themselves constitute an ecclesiastical office; election/calling does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers of the Word (Christ's ministers) vs Ministers of the Church (diakonos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek diakonos signifies one who voluntarily does another's business: both preachers and deacons are 'Ministers' but of different persons — Pastors are Ministers of Christ (the Word); Deacons minister to the Congregation (serving tables, secular affairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain functions (e.g., conferring the Holy Ghost) required a Minister of the Word; Philip the Deacon baptized but the Apostles (Ministers of the Word) had to confirm with imposition of hands for the Holy Ghost to accompany believers, illustrating functional distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of hands is an ancient consecratory ceremony but not an absolute ontological requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of Hands was an ancient public ceremony to designate or consecrate persons/things, used in priestly and leadership actions in Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although historically important (Jacob blessing, Moses ordaining Joshua, Levites consecration), its absence does not necessarily bar the civil sovereign from exercising baptism/consecration: sovereign authority may authorize pastoral acts even without ordinary ritual imposition, and practical delegation explains why kings rarely perform such rites themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of ministers originally by voluntary benevolence, not fixed tithes
rubrics_metrics.description: In apostolic times ministers lived on voluntary contributions ('the Free Gift of those that beleeved'); there was no certain maintenance assigned except by possessions, labour, and voluntary contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tithes and fixed allowances under Moses derived from the civil-king system (Levi's inheritance being the tenth). Thus the right of tithes is a civil arrangement; only when civil sovereigns enacted settlements could certain revenues be assigned to ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of tithes and ecclesiastical revenue is derived from civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Old Testament the Levites' maintenance (tithes, oblations) was constituted by the civil/political order (God as King and Moses/Aaron as lieutenants); similarly, church livings and tithes in later times are determined by civil sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because public revenue is at the disposing of the public person (sovereign), rights to tithes and offerings are civilly constituted; after the return from Captivity and until later civil regulation, maintenance practices derived from civil context and sovereign decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign as Supreme Pastor (de jure divino); other pastors operate jure civili
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Christian Sovereign is the Supreme Pastor of his own subjects by immediate authority from God (Dei Gratia / de jure divino), while all other pastors execute their office by the authority of the civil sovereign (jure civili).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus pastors should acknowledge civil subjection in their titles/mandates; the King may lawfully ordain and appoint pastors, and the pastoral right of kings is necessary for public peace and governance. The crown's pastoral power includes choosing teachers for subjects and withdrawing them if against the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian sovereigns have power to perform pastoral functions (preach, baptize, consecrate) though custom and practical delegation limit this
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sovereign is Supreme Pastor, he has authority to preach, baptize, administer sacraments, and consecrate persons/places, even if in practice he delegates these duties because of other governmental burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative reasons: Jesus and Paul, though able to baptize, sent others due to greater charges (preaching/governance). Practical governance explains why kings rarely personally perform sacraments; delegation does not negate their underlying authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of Deacons by the Congregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deacons (first seven) were chosen by the congregation of disciples (the multitude) after the Apostles proposed criteria, i.e., the people selected 'seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost, and of Wisdome.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts 6 example: Apostles set criteria and presided, but 'the saying pleased the multitude, and they chose seven.' This demonstrates that even ministerial officers were elected by the faithful assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical censure (excommunication) defined relative to civil law
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical Censure (excommunication) is putting a person out of the company of the excommunicate where Christianity is forbidden by civil laws, or excluding them from congregations where Christianity is commanded by civil law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excommunication's force and meaning depend on the civil context: where Christian worship is illegal it means social/external exclusion; where civil law supports Christianity it entails being put out of the congregation. Thus censure interacts with civil enforcement.
